title: IF GOD IS REALLY WITH ME, WHY IS MY LIFE FALLING APART?
paragraphs: IF GOD IS REALLY WITH ME, WHY IS MY LIFE FALLING APART?
Gideon Asked the Question Many Christians Are Afraid to Say Out Loud — And God's Answer Was More Powerful Than the Miracle He Was Praying For.
“If the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us?” — Judges 6:13 (KJV)
There is a kind of pain that makes you cry.
And then there is a kind of pain that makes you question everything you thought you knew about God.
Not because you stopped believing in Him.
But because you believed.
You prayed. You trusted. You tried to do what was right. You held on when other people would have walked away.
And somehow, despite all of that, your life still fell apart.
The marriage you prayed over is breaking.
The child you raised to know Jesus is walking away from Him.
The bills are piling up, the diagnosis has changed everything, the people you trusted have disappointed you, and the prayers you whispered through tears seem to have disappeared into the ceiling.
You still attend church.
You still say, "God is good."
You still encourage people to trust Him.
But somewhere underneath your Sunday smile is a question you have been terrified to admit.
Lord, if You are really with me, why am I going through this?
What if I told you that one of the men God chose to deliver Israel asked almost exactly the same question?
And what if the most astonishing part of his story wasn't that God eventually gave him victory...
But that God came looking for him while he was still hiding?
His name was Gideon.
And before he became a mighty warrior, he was a frightened man trying to survive another terrible day.
The Bible doesn't introduce Gideon standing on a battlefield, holding a sword, surrounded by cheering soldiers.
It introduces him hiding in a winepress.
Not praying down fire from heaven.
Not declaring victory over his enemies.
Not demonstrating extraordinary courage.
Just hiding.
Trying to keep a little wheat from being stolen.
And perhaps that is why his story feels painfully familiar.
Because sometimes the person God is calling is not the person standing confidently in front of everyone.
Sometimes it is the person quietly falling apart where nobody can see.
Israel had been suffering under Midianite oppression for seven years.
Seven years.
Imagine what seven years of fear can do to a family.
Every harvest carried the threat of destruction. Every season of planting came with the possibility that someone stronger would take everything.
Judges 6:3–6 describes how Midian and its allies invaded Israel's land, devastated its crops, and left the people impoverished.
Families fled into mountain dens, caves, and strongholds.
People who had inherited a land of promise were living like fugitives in their own country.
And there was a reason for this suffering that the biblical narrator refuses to hide.
Judges 6:1 says:
"And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD: and the LORD delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years." (KJV)
This matters.
Because if we turn Gideon's story into nothing more than a motivational speech about overcoming adversity, we miss the uncomfortable truth at its center.
Israel was not simply an innocent nation experiencing random misfortune.
The people had turned away from the God who delivered them.
They had embraced the very idolatry God warned them against.
And their suffering was connected to covenant unfaithfulness.
But before you assume that every hardship in your own life must be punishment for some hidden sin, remember something equally important.
The Bible does not teach that every tragedy is the direct consequence of a person's wrongdoing.
Jesus explicitly rejected that assumption in John 9:1–3 when His disciples asked whether a man's blindness resulted from his sin or his parents' sin.
Sometimes suffering exposes sin.
Sometimes suffering comes because we live in a fallen world.
Sometimes suffering comes precisely because we belong to Christ.
And sometimes we simply do not know why God has permitted what He has permitted.
We must never pretend to know what Scripture has not revealed.
But in Gideon's particular story, God had already explained Israel's national crisis.
Before the angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon, God sent a prophet to remind Israel of His deliverance from Egypt and of the people's refusal to obey His voice.
God had not forgotten His covenant.
Israel had forgotten its God.
And yet...
In the middle of that rebellion, God came near.
Read that again.
God came near.
Not because Israel had finally become impressive.
Not because Gideon had demonstrated heroic faith.
But because the God of Scripture is merciful, even when His people have been unfaithful.
Judges 6:11 tells us Gideon was threshing wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites.
Wheat was normally threshed in an open place where the wind could help separate the grain from the chaff.
But Gideon was working in concealment.
Fear had changed the way he lived.
Fear had reduced his world.
Fear had made survival more urgent than anything resembling greatness.
And that is where the angel of the LORD found him.
Then came a greeting so unexpected that it almost sounds impossible.
"The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." — Judges 6:12 (KJV)
Mighty man of valor?
Gideon?
The man hiding from the enemy?
The man protecting a little wheat because he was afraid of losing it?
Yes.
And Gideon's response was not a triumphant declaration of faith.
It was a question.
A wounded, searching, deeply human question.
"Oh my Lord, if the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us? and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of...?" — Judges 6:13 (KJV)
Can you hear the ache?
If God is with us, why are we suffering?
If the stories about His power are true, where is that power now?
If He delivered our fathers, why are we hiding from our enemies?
Gideon had heard the testimonies.
He knew the history.
He knew about Egypt.
He knew about the God who brought His people out of slavery.
But knowing what God had done for previous generations was not the same as understanding what God was doing in his own.
And that is where so many believers struggle.
We hear testimonies of marriages restored while our own homes are collapsing.
We hear about miraculous provision while checking a bank account that cannot cover next week's expenses.
We hear about answered prayers while standing beside a hospital bed.
We read about deliverance while fighting the same temptation we promised God we would never return to.
And quietly, almost ashamed of ourselves, we wonder:
Where are the miracles now?
The Hebrew wording of Gideon's question makes the moment even more striking.
The phrase translated "why then is all this befallen us?" includes:
וְלָמָּה מְצָאַתְנוּ כָּל־זֹאת
Ve-lammah metza'atnu kol-zot.
The sense is, "And why has all this happened to us?" or more literally, "Why has all this found us?"
The Hebrew verb comes from מָצָא (matsa), meaning "to find" or "to encounter."
Gideon is looking at the devastation surrounding his people and asking why these things have overtaken them if the LORD is truly with them.
This is not the polished language of someone who has figured everything out.
It is the language of a man struggling to reconcile God's promised presence with the painful reality before his eyes.
And here is something remarkable.
God did not answer Gideon by giving him a complete explanation of every painful event.
The explanation of Israel's covenant failure had already been delivered through the prophet.
Instead, God turned Gideon's attention toward what He was about to do.
Judges 6:14 says:
"And the LORD looked upon him, and said, Go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites: have not I sent thee?" (KJV)
Notice that.
Gideon asked why.
God answered with a calling.
Gideon looked at what had happened.
God directed him toward what was coming.
But this does not mean that every suffering Christian will receive a dramatic assignment, a military victory, or a sudden reversal of circumstances.
Gideon's calling was specific to Gideon.
His story is not a promise that every believer will defeat an earthly enemy.
It reveals something deeper about the character of God.
The LORD had not abandoned His redemptive purposes.
And the weakness of the person He called would not prevent Him from accomplishing those purposes.
Still, Gideon was not convinced.
He answered:
"Oh my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel? behold, my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house." — Judges 6:15 (KJV)
There it is.
The voice of inadequacy.
The voice that says, "You must have chosen the wrong person."
The voice that remembers every failure, every weakness, every reason someone else would be better qualified.
Gideon saw his family position.
God saw the mission He was entrusting to him.
Gideon saw his insufficiency.
God declared His presence.
And the LORD answered him with words that would become the foundation of everything that followed:
"Surely I will be with thee." — Judges 6:16 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the promise begins:
כִּי אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ
Ki ehyeh immakh.
"For I will be with you."
The verb אֶהְיֶה (ehyeh) is related to the Hebrew verb "to be."
The wording recalls God's promise to Moses in Exodus 3:12, when Moses also felt inadequate for the assignment before him.
God did not tell Gideon that he was naturally powerful enough.
He promised that Gideon would not face his calling alone.
That distinction changes everything.
Because the foundation of Gideon's victory was never Gideon's greatness.
It was God's presence.
And perhaps you need to hear this today.
Your weakness does not surprise God.
Your limitations do not intimidate Him.
Your tears do not make you useless.
But neither does God's presence mean that every frightening circumstance will immediately disappear.
The same God who promised Gideon His presence later led him through a process that required obedience, courage, patience, and trust.
Gideon still had to confront the idolatry in his father's household.
He still struggled with fear.
He still sought reassurance.
He still had to face an enemy army that vastly outnumbered his own.
And before the battle, God did something that seemed completely unreasonable.
He reduced Gideon's army.
From thirty-two thousand men to ten thousand.
Then from ten thousand to just three hundred.
Why?
Judges 7:2 gives the reason.
God would not allow Israel to claim that its own strength had saved it.
The victory would belong to the LORD.
Imagine standing in Gideon's place.
You have finally gathered an army.
You have finally found enough courage to move forward.
And God begins removing the very resources you were counting on.
Would you still trust Him?
It is easy to praise God when the numbers are increasing.
When the opportunities are multiplying.
When the bank account is growing.
When the medical results are improving.
But what happens when things become smaller?
When the support you expected disappears?
When the future looks less secure than it did yesterday?
Gideon's story reminds us that God's ability to save is not measured by the resources we can count.
But be careful not to twist that truth.
It does not mean that every financial loss, broken relationship, or personal disappointment is God secretly reducing your army.
Scripture does not give us permission to interpret every painful event that way.
What it does show is that when God has made a promise, human weakness cannot overturn His faithfulness.
And that brings us to something Gideon had to confront before he ever faced Midian.
The altar of Baal.
In Judges 6:25–32, God commanded Gideon to tear down his father's altar to Baal and cut down the Asherah pole beside it.
The problem was not only the enemy outside Israel.
There was rebellion within Israel.
The people wanted deliverance from Midian while tolerating the idols that had drawn their hearts away from the LORD.
That is a difficult truth.
Because sometimes we want God to change our circumstances without allowing Him to confront what is happening inside us.
We ask Him to restore our peace while refusing to surrender the bitterness we keep feeding.
We ask Him to heal our relationships while protecting the pride that keeps us from apologizing.
We ask Him to free us from destructive patterns while quietly making room for the same temptations.
We want rescue.
But repentance feels costly.
Yet the Gospel does not invite us merely to escape the consequences of sin.
It calls us to turn from sin and return to God.
Repentance is not a payment that purchases God's mercy.
It is the proper response to the mercy of the God who calls sinners back to Himself.
And Gideon's story contains another detail that makes it painfully real.
He obeyed God's command to tear down the altar.
But he did it at night.
Judges 6:27 explains that Gideon feared his father's household and the men of the city.
He was still afraid.
Even while obeying.
Do not miss that.
The man God called a mighty warrior did not instantly become fearless.
He took a step of obedience while fear was still present.
Some of you have been waiting to feel courageous before doing what you know is right.
Waiting until you are no longer afraid to confess the truth.
Waiting until you feel strong enough to walk away from the sin that keeps dragging you back.
Waiting until you feel worthy enough to return to prayer.
But obedience does not always begin with confidence.
Sometimes it begins with trembling hands.
Sometimes it begins with a whispered confession.
Sometimes it begins with one honest sentence:
Jesus, I cannot keep living like this. Please help me.
And then comes one of the most beautiful moments in Gideon's story.
Before Gideon led Israel into battle, he built an altar to the LORD.
He named it:
יְהוָה שָׁלוֹם
YHWH Shalom.
"The LORD is peace."
Judges 6:24.
Not "The LORD has already removed every enemy."
Not "The LORD has made my circumstances comfortable."
Not "The LORD has explained everything."
The LORD is peace.
And the context matters.
Gideon had feared for his life after realizing that he had encountered the angel of the LORD.
But God reassured him:
"Peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die." — Judges 6:23 (KJV)
The Hebrew word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) carries the sense of peace and well-being, often associated with wholeness and welfare.
In this passage, God's declaration directly reassured Gideon that he would not die from the encounter.
The altar's name celebrated the LORD as the source of that peace.
The Midianites were still there.
The battle had not yet been fought.
The danger had not vanished.
Yet Gideon had received a word of peace from God.
And here is where the story begins pointing us toward something even greater than Gideon.
Because Gideon could deliver Israel from Midian for a time.
But he could not deliver humanity from sin.
He could win a battle.
But he could not conquer death.
He could tear down an altar to Baal.
But he could not give the world a new heart.
Israel needed more than another judge.
The world needed a Savior.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ came.
Not merely to rescue one nation from an invading army.
But to save sinners from the guilt and dominion of sin, reconcile us to God, and defeat death through His resurrection.
Gideon's story is part of the larger biblical history that leads us to Christ.

And while we should not force every detail of Gideon's life into a hidden prediction about Jesus, the contrast between the temporary deliverance of Israel's judges and the ultimate salvation accomplished by Christ is unmistakable.
Gideon was weak and needed God to rescue him.
Jesus is the sinless Son of God who came to rescue us.
Gideon feared death.
Jesus willingly went to the cross.
Gideon's victory brought relief from oppression.
Christ's death and resurrection opened the way to everlasting reconciliation with God.
And here is the part that should stop you in your tracks.
The God who came near to Gideon in his hiding place has revealed His saving grace decisively in Jesus Christ.
Not because humanity deserved it.
Not because we had finally become righteous.
But because of His mercy.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired everything.
Not after we learned to pray beautifully.
Not after we conquered every temptation.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
Think about that.
Gideon was hiding from Midian.
But humanity's deeper problem was never merely the enemy standing outside the door.
It was the sin that separated us from a holy God.
And Jesus did what no earthly deliverer could ever accomplish.
He bore our sins in His body on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The resurrection is not a sentimental ending added to a tragic story.
It is the decisive victory of the risen Christ.
And because He lives, everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith has a hope that suffering cannot finally destroy.
That does not mean Christians never grieve.
It does not mean every illness is healed in this life.
It does not mean every marriage is restored or every financial burden disappears.
Jesus Himself told His disciples that they would have tribulation in this world.
But He also said:
"Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world." — John 16:33 (KJV)
The Christian promise is not that we will never walk through darkness.
It is that darkness will not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And perhaps this is the part of Gideon's question we need to reconsider.
He asked:
If the LORD is with us, why has all this happened?
But the presence of suffering was not proof that God had ceased to exist, that His covenant purposes had failed, or that His mercy had run out.
Israel's sin was real.
God's discipline was real.
Their suffering was real.
And God's compassion was real too.
Those truths existed together.
Just as the cross of Jesus Christ reveals both the terrible seriousness of sin and the astonishing greatness of divine love.
At Calvary, the disciples witnessed what must have seemed like the collapse of everything they hoped for.
Their Teacher was arrested.
Their Lord was condemned.
Their Messiah was crucified.
And for a moment, the story appeared to end in defeat.
But the tomb did not remain occupied.
The resurrection revealed that what looked like the triumph of evil had become the place where God's saving purpose was accomplished.
And no, that does not mean every tragedy in your life is secretly a blessing.
Some losses are genuinely devastating.
Some wounds leave scars.
Some questions remain unanswered this side of eternity.
Christian faith does not require you to call evil good.
It calls you to trust the God who raised Jesus from the dead, even when you cannot understand everything He permits.
That is a different kind of hope.
A hope that does not depend on pretending everything is fine.
A hope that can sit beside a hospital bed and weep.
A hope that can stand at a graveside and grieve.
A hope that can confess, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."
A hope that keeps looking toward Christ.
And maybe you are reading this because you have been living inside your own winepress.
Not a literal one.
But a place of hiding.
A place where you have learned to keep your pain quiet.
Where you encourage everyone else while secretly wondering how much longer you can hold on.
Where you have convinced yourself that real Christians never struggle with difficult questions.
Listen carefully.
Gideon's question was recorded in Scripture.
God did not erase it from the story.
The Bible is honest about human fear, weakness, doubt, rebellion, and the mercy of God.
But Gideon's story also warns us not to remain forever in the posture of accusation.
His question was not the end of his encounter with God.
The LORD called him to respond.
To trust.
To turn away from idolatry.
To obey.
To move forward in dependence upon divine strength.
And perhaps that is where this story meets you today.
Not with a promise that your problems will vanish tomorrow.
But with an invitation to stop running from the One who can save your soul.
Maybe you need to repent of a sin you have been defending.
Maybe you need to stop pretending your faith is stronger than it is.
Maybe you need to ask forgiveness from someone you have wounded.
Maybe you need to forgive someone while wisely maintaining necessary boundaries.
Maybe you need to open your Bible again after months of silence.
Maybe you need to ask a trusted pastor or mature believer to pray with you because you are tired of carrying everything alone.
Or maybe you simply need to tell Jesus the truth.
Lord, I am hurting.
I do not understand.
I have questions.
But I do not want to walk away from You.
There is no shame in bringing an honest lament before God.
The Psalms are filled with cries of anguish.
Yet biblical lament is more than expressing pain.
It brings that pain into the presence of God and seeks His mercy.
And the invitation of the Gospel is even greater.
Come to Jesus.
Not merely for a better week.
Not merely for a breakthrough.
Not merely for relief from your circumstances.
Come to Him because He is the Savior you need, whether your circumstances improve quickly or not.
Come in repentance.
Come in faith.
Come trusting His death and resurrection rather than your own goodness.
Because the deepest miracle is not that Gideon eventually defeated Midian.
The deepest miracle available to a sinner is to be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new through Jesus Christ.
That is not just a beautiful phrase.
It is the testimony of the Gospel.
The scandal of human rebellion.
The shame of sin.
The brokenness we cannot repair by ourselves.
And the grace of God revealed through the crucified and risen Christ.
Grace that does not excuse sin but forgives repentant sinners.
Grace that does not leave us unchanged but teaches us to walk in holiness.
Grace that reaches people in places they never expected mercy to find them.
Perhaps your story has chapters you wish you could erase.
Perhaps you carry regrets that still make your stomach tighten when you remember them.
Perhaps you are ashamed of the person you used to be.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your past does not have the authority to overturn His saving work.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
That promise is not about pretending the past never happened.
It is about the new life God gives through union with Christ.
The scars may remain.
The consequences of some choices may still need to be faced.
Restitution may be necessary.
Trust may need time to be rebuilt.
But forgiveness is real.
Redemption is real.
Transformation is real.
And Jesus Christ is alive.
So before you leave this article, I want to ask you something.
Not as a religious performance.
Not to impress anyone.
Not because writing a sentence in a comment section can save your soul.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes the first step toward honest fellowship is admitting what we have been afraid to say.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to share.
But your honest words may remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And if Jesus has already brought you through a season when you thought your faith would collapse, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Not to make yourself the hero.
But to glorify the Savior who sustained you.
Someone reading the comments may need that reminder tonight.
And please, do not let this message stop with you.
Not merely because it helps a page grow, but because someone among your family, friends, coworkers, or acquaintances may be silently asking Gideon's question.
Someone may have stopped praying.
Someone may be close to abandoning church.
Someone may believe their failures have placed them beyond the reach of grace.
Your simple act of sharing could place a Scripture-centered message in front of someone who would never have searched for it.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are growing weary, Christians who have grown spiritually complacent, and even those who do not yet know Jesus.
Not everyone will respond immediately.
But the Word of God is worth sharing faithfully.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront sin, or draw nearer to Jesus Christ, I want to invite you into something deeper.
This is not about buying God's favor.
It is not about paying for forgiveness.
And it is certainly not about purchasing a blessing.
But meaningful Gospel ministry does require time, resources, faithful labor, and people who are willing to help carry the work forward.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)

But if you believe in this mission, if these messages have nourished your faith, and if you desire to help make Scripture-centered content available to more people, your partnership can make a meaningful difference.
Think about the believer who is too ashamed to ask a question in church.
The young person who is quietly losing faith.
The parent who cries after everyone else has gone to sleep.
The person who has never opened a Bible but encounters a Gospel message while scrolling through Facebook.
We cannot know in advance whose heart God may reach through a particular article.
But we can faithfully proclaim Christ and make His Word accessible.
These products are simply expressions of encouragement and gratitude, not spiritual rewards or measures of anyone's faith.
Those free resources are part of the heart of this mission.
We want believers to read.
To study.
To examine the Scriptures.
To grow in discernment.
To know the Gospel.
And above all, to know Jesus Christ more deeply.
Not out of guilt.
Not out of fear.
Not because you think God will love you more.
But because you want to participate in sharing biblical truth and making discipleship resources available to others.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share Scripture matters.
Your faithful witness in everyday life matters.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
And He alone deserves the glory.
Now, return with me for one final moment to that frightened man in the winepress.
Gideon.
The man who asked why everything had gone wrong.
The man who thought his weakness disqualified him.
The man who needed repeated reassurance.
The man who could not yet see what God was preparing to do.
When God first addressed him, Gideon was hiding.
When God promised His presence, Gideon was uncertain.
When God commanded him to tear down the altar, Gideon was afraid.
But the story did not end in the winepress.
And neither must your story end in the place where fear found you.
Not because you are guaranteed Gideon's circumstances or Gideon's victory.
But because through Jesus Christ, there is forgiveness for sinners, strength for obedience, hope for the suffering, and resurrection life beyond the grave.
Maybe your questions are still unanswered.
Maybe the grief is still fresh.
Maybe the circumstances you prayed about have not changed.
You do not have to manufacture a smile.
You do not have to pretend you are fearless.
You do not have to invent a testimony before God has brought you through the trial.
But you can turn toward Christ today.
You can confess your sin.
You can bring Him your grief.
You can trust His promises.
You can ask Him for strength to take the next faithful step.
And you can remember that the greatest evidence of God's love is not the absence of suffering in your life.
It is Jesus Christ crucified and risen for sinners.
The same Jesus who said:
"I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee." — Hebrews 13:5 (KJV)
The same Jesus who promised His disciples:
"Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world." — Matthew 28:20 (KJV)
So when your heart asks, "If God is with me, why has all this happened?"
Do not silence the question with a shallow answer.
Bring it to the cross.
Bring it to the empty tomb.
Bring it to the Savior who knows what suffering is.
And even when you cannot understand the chapter you are living through, hold fast to the One who has promised eternal life to those who trust in Him.
Because the final word over a redeemed life does not belong to shame.
It does not belong to sin.
It does not belong to the grave.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
The winepress may be where fear found Gideon, but it was not where God's calling left him. And the grave may be where the world thought Jesus' story ended, but the stone was rolled away.
